passages.t: A luxuriant vine, and a calf carried off
passages.happening:
‘Israel was a luxuriant vine, yielding fruit for himself’ (verse 1). The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built. The better his land produced, the finer he made his sacred pillars. Their hearts are false, and the LORD will break down their altars (verse 2). Soon they will say they have no king, because they do not fear the LORD, and what could a king do for them anyway (verse 3)? They make covenants with false oaths, and judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in a field (verse 4).

The people of Samaria will tremble for the calf of Beth-aven, and its priests will mourn, ‘for it has been taken from them into exile’ (verse 5). ‘Yes, it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king’ (verse 6). Samaria and her king will be carried off ‘like a twig on the surface of the water’ (verse 7). The high places will be destroyed, and thorns and thistles will grow over the altars. Then they will call on the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Sacred pillars, standing stones, were common at Canaanite shrines and had been forbidden to Israel. Hosea's point is that Israel treated its rising wealth as a reason to build more of them, turning God's gifts into occasions for idolatry. The vine grew, and so did the altars.

The calf at Bethel had stood since Jeroboam I set it up nearly two centuries earlier as a rival to the temple in Jerusalem. Hosea says this prized object, which could not save anyone, will be hauled off to Assyria as tribute. The great king may echo an Assyrian royal title. Beth-aven, house of wickedness or house of nothing, is his bitter pun on Bethel, house of God. The word for the calf's priests is a word used only for priests of false gods.

The line about having no king may reflect the turmoil after Jeroboam II, when four kings were murdered within about twenty years, or the moment Assyria imprisoned Hoshea, Israel's last king. A twig on the water is swept away without a sound.
passages.later: Jesus used the words of verse 8 on his way to the cross, warning the women of Jerusalem of days when people would say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us’ (Luke 23:30). Revelation uses the same words for the last day (Revelation 6:16).
passages.asks: Israel's prosperity led to more altars, not more faithfulness. Ask what your good years have done to your love for God. And ask what you have treasured that could be carried off like the calf of Bethel.

passages.happening:
‘Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel, and there you have remained’ (verse 9). God will discipline them, and nations will gather against them (verse 10). Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh, but God will put a yoke on her neck. Judah will plow, and Jacob will break the hard ground (verse 11).

‘Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground. For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain’ (verse 12). Instead, ‘You have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies’ (verse 13), because they trusted in their own way and their many warriors. So the roar of battle will rise against them, and their fortresses will be destroyed, as when Shalman laid waste Beth-arbel in a day of war (verse 14). So it will be done to Bethel, and at dawn Israel's king will be cut off (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The days of Gibeah recall the rape and murder at Gibeah and the civil war that followed, a low point Israel never forgot.

The farm pictures come from daily life. A heifer threshing grain walked unmuzzled over the sheaves and could eat as she worked, so threshing was light and pleasant. Plowing under a yoke was hard labor. Ephraim has enjoyed the easy work and will now be put under the yoke. Unplowed ground was fallow land grown hard, which had to be broken before seed could take root. The heart of the chapter is the contrast between two ways of sowing: righteousness that brings a harvest of loving devotion, or wickedness that brings injustice.

Verse 14 recalls a massacre that Hosea's hearers knew, though it is not recorded anywhere else. Some scholars identify Shalman with an Assyrian king named Shalmaneser, others with Salamanu, a ruler of Moab named in an Assyrian list of tribute. Beth-arbel may be Irbid in Gilead or a town in Galilee. The identification is uncertain.
passages.later: The law let the ox eat while it threshed (Deuteronomy 25:4). Jeremiah took up Hosea's call: ‘Break up your unplowed ground, and do not sow among the thorns’ (Jeremiah 4:3).
passages.hard:
Why does Hosea mention mothers and children in verse 14?

Verse 14 names one of the horrors of ancient siege warfare, when conquerors killed whole populations. The verse is named here and not described. Hosea is not approving it. He is recalling a massacre his hearers remembered, and warning that the same cruelty will fall on Israel when Assyria comes. The prophets condemn such atrocities as crimes when other nations commit them, as Amos does (Amos 1:13), while also saying that God will let Israel suffer them because it trusted in its own strength. Some interpreters stress that God's judgment works through human armies who remain guilty of their own cruelty. Others stress that the prophets' honesty about war strips away any romance about trusting in military power, which is what verse 13 condemns.

This is Israel's own Scripture, spoken by its own prophet to his own people. It gives no warrant for violence against anyone, and no key for calling any people's suffering in war, then or now, deserved.
passages.asks: Hosea gives two ways of sowing. Ask what you are sowing in your relationships, and what it will grow. And ask where the ground of your heart has gone hard and needs breaking up so that God can plant something new.
